test_description: Bare collection title, minimally specified. The corpus contains exactly 38 volumes titled 'Courses and degrees. 19XX-19XX', running consecutively from 1957-58 through 1994-95 with no gaps (confirmed against the collection facet count of 38; there is no 1955-56 or 1956-57 volume, and the series stops after 1994-95). Every one of those 38 is an exact title match and is scored 3 — the case is graded across the whole series rather than a sample of it, so recall over the series is measurable and not just precision at the top. The real stress is lexical collision: 'courses' and 'degrees' are two of the most common tokens in an academic corpus, and keyword search reports 2,778 total matches for this query. The near-misses to watch are the 'Announcement of courses' series (51 volumes, 1907-1955), the direct predecessor publication under a different title, and the 'Annual register' and later 'Stanford bulletin' series, which carry the same content type under yet other titles. A healthy result set is 38 titled volumes and nothing else; a run that interleaves Announcement of courses, Annual register or Stanford Bulletin into the top ranks has let common-token overlap outrank an exact title match. Note that rows is capped at 20 per request, so a full-series evaluation of this case needs pagination or repeated probes.

query: What was the first law degree offered by the Stanford School of Law in the 1960s?

query: military and naval training for undergraduates on campus
test_description: Abstract theme with no corpus vocabulary borrowed from the target documents. The 1960s 'Courses and degrees' volumes are textbook instances of this theme — their contents pages list 'Military Science', 'Naval Science' and 'Aerospace Studies' as full departments with course-by-course descriptions, and ROTC was only phased out at Stanford in 1973. This case tests whether documents *about* the subject outrank documents merely *discussing* it. It currently fails hard: a hybrid run returned Campus report volumes (news articles reflecting on ROTC), Annual register 1917-1919, Announcement of courses 1918-1930 and an alumni oral-history interview, and did not surface a single 1960s 'Courses and degrees' volume in the top ten. The World War I-era material scores high because it uses the theme's exact words ('MILITARY TRAINING' as a section heading, 'Reserve Officers Training Corps'), while the 1960s catalogs describe the same programs under the drier institutional labels 'Naval Science' and 'Military Science'. The failure mode is vocabulary-era mismatch, not topical error.

judgments.explanation: 'Courses and degrees. 1964-1965' is an instance of the theme: pages 340-341 carry the full Naval Science curriculum ('111. ROTC programs were finally phased out at Stanford in 1973'), but it is a news account discussing the programs retrospectively, not a document listing the training itself.

'Campus report. Volume 3, 1970-1971' reports the Academic Council vote and the Navy's plan to phase out NROTC by June 1973 — substantively about undergraduate military training on campus, but again commentary rather than the curriculum.

'Annual register. 1918-1919' contains an extensive MILITARY TRAINING section with the ROTC infantry unit and summer instruction camps. It matches the query's words better than any 1960s volume, but it is a different serial from a different era; defensible as a neighbour, and worth documenting as the reason the target decade gets displaced.
'Announcement of courses. 1918-1919' — same reasoning: verbatim 'MILITARY TRAINING' heading and R.O.T.C. prose from the predecessor series, forty years before the queried decades.
'Announcement of courses. 1930-1931' lists 'MILITARY SCIENCE AND TACTICS' with the R.O.T.C. basic and advanced courses. Right theme, wrong series and era.

'Interview with Richard Anderson : Alumni Stories'. Retrieved because a reminiscence about NROTC drills matches the theme's surface language ('we drilled on a practice field... we carried rifles'), but an oral-history transcript is not a record of instruction offered and answers no part of the underlying need.
'Annual register. 1917-1918'. Wartime military-training prose; a false positive on era, driven by the heading 'MILITARY, PHYSICAL TRAINING' rather than by any relation to the 1960s-80s catalogs.

query: undergraduate degree requirements in the 1974-1975 Stanford bulletin, printed book, in English
test_description: Topic (undergraduate degree requirements) + date (1974-1975) + format (printed book) + language (English). The format and language facets live in structured fields — the corpus exposes format_hsim 'Book' and a collection facet — while the date lives only in the title string and in scattered calendar chunks. A hybrid run does get the target to rank 1, matching the DEGREES section on page 9, which is a better result than the keyword path can manage (keyword search ignores year tokens entirely here). But the run also reports 39,440 total matches and fills ranks 3, 4, 6, 8, 9 and 10 with 'Stanford Bulletin' volumes from 2003-2012, which satisfy topic, format and language while violating the date constraint by three decades — and which the query arguably invites by using the word 'bulletin'. The tradeoff this case exposes: the embedding treats the date as soft context, so a stricter test is whether the system can be made to filter on it rather than merely rank by it.

query: When were freshmen encouraged to complete the Western Culture requirement?
test_description: A 1980s question whose answer — during the freshman year, though deferral was permitted — appears in a boilerplate paragraph repeated with only the year changed across the 1983-84 through 1986-87 volumes. Because the paragraph is near-verbatim across volumes, the retriever will return several of them and the only thing distinguishing them is the embedded year string ('The following courses are available in 1983-84' / '1984-85' / '1986-87'). That makes this a good test of whether an answer-bearing chunk can be attributed to the right volume. The distractors are the individual Western Culture track descriptions (Great Works, Structured Liberal Education, Ideas in Western Culture, Conflict and Change, Literature and the Arts, Western Culture and Technology), which dominate similarity scores for anything mentioning Western Culture but state track content rather than timing. Volumes from 1989-90 onward are the period trap: by then the requirement had been replaced by Cultures, Ideas, and Values (CIV), so they cannot answer the question.
